text: Around 300 million years ago, Earth's air probably held a lot more oxygen than it does now, possibly up to about 30% or more instead of today's 21%. Many scientists think this let insects grow much bigger.

Insects don't have lungs. Air seeps into their bodies through a network of fine tubes. The bigger an insect gets, the longer those tubes must be, and the harder it is to get enough oxygen deep inside. With more oxygen in the air, each breath went further, so giant bodies could still get enough. Some winged insects of the time had wingspans of about 70 cm, about as wide as a pigeon's.

st.prompt: How do insects get oxygen into their bodies?

options.t: Through tiny tubes that run from holes in their sides

st.reveal: Insects have small holes along their bodies called spiracles. These lead into a network of tubes called tracheae, which carry air straight to the muscles. Air moves through them slowly, which may limit how big an insect can grow.

sec.t:
This time is called the Carboniferous period, meaning "coal-bearing". Huge swampy forests covered much of the land. Trees were often giant relatives of ferns and horsetails, some taller than a 10-storey building.

These plants pumped oxygen into the air. When they died, many fell into swamps and never fully rotted away, because few microbes could yet break down wood. Over millions of years, they were buried and turned into the [[@oil-coal|coal]] that powers many factories and power stations today. That buried carbon may also explain why oxygen levels rose so high.

Crawling below them was *Arthropleura*, a millipede relative up to about 2.6 m long and about 50 cm wide. It was longer than a small car. Its fossil tracks, some as wide as a tyre, have been found in Scotland and North America. In 2024, scientists studying well-preserved fossils found that it had eyes on stalks, like a crab.

Some scorpions of the time grew to about 70 cm long, and a few mayflies had wings wider than your hand.

The oxygen idea has strong support. In laboratory tests, some insects raised in extra-oxygen air grew bigger over several generations. And when oxygen levels dropped later, giant insects seem to have disappeared.

The last griffinflies vanished around 252 million years ago, in the [[@great-dying|Great Dying]]. That disaster, probably caused by enormous volcanic eruptions in Siberia, wiped out most living species on land and in the sea. Insects bounced back, but the giants never returned.

But it may not be the whole story. When the giants lived, there were no birds, no bats and no flying reptiles. Nothing in the air could chase a big, slow insect. Later, as flying hunters appeared, smaller and nimbler insects survived better. Many scientists now think both oxygen and predators mattered.

Insects are still pretty big in some places. The Goliath beetle of Africa can weigh about as much as a tennis ball when it is a grub. The Atlas moth of South and Southeast Asia, found in India's northeast and Western Ghats, has wings up to about 25 cm across. Some stick insects in Borneo and China grow longer than 55 cm with their legs stretched.

They are still nowhere near the size of a griffinfly. The age of giant insects ended long ago, but millions of years later, another giant ruled the swamps, as the story of [[@lost-titanoboa|Titanoboa]] shows.

text: A salt flat is a wide, flat stretch of ground covered with a crust of salt. Most are the beds of ancient lakes that dried up. Rivers had been carrying tiny amounts of dissolved [[@salt|salt]] into these lakes for thousands of years. When the water evaporated, the salt stayed, and layer by layer it built a white floor that can be many metres thick.

The biggest is Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia, high in the Andes mountains, at about 10,500 km². Others include the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, USA, and the salt marshes of the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, India.

st.prompt: How did most salt flats form?

options.t: Ancient lakes dried up and left their dissolved salt behind
Seawater was blown inland by storms
Salt crystals grew up out of underground rock

st.reveal: Rivers carry small amounts of dissolved salt into lakes with no outlet. When the climate dries and the water evaporates, the salt stays behind. Over thousands of years it builds into a hard white crust.

Many salt flats are full of life at the edges or in their shallow lakes. Uyuni's lagoons host flamingos, and the Rann of Kutch is home to the Indian wild ass and huge flamingo breeding colonies.

sec.t:
Around the edges of Uyuni, some hotels are built from blocks of salt cut from the flat. Walls, beds, tables and chairs are all salt. Guests are politely asked not to lick the walls.

Underneath the crust is something far more valuable: brine, very salty water rich in lithium. Lithium goes into the rechargeable [[@batteries-phones|batteries]] in phones, laptops and electric cars. Bolivia has some of the largest known lithium resources on Earth, and companies and governments are working out how to extract it without harming the water supply of nearby communities.

The Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah are what's left of a giant ancient lake, Lake Bonneville, that once covered much of the area around 15,000 years ago. Today the salt is hard and smooth enough to drive on. Since the early 1900s, people have raced cars there to set land speed records, and a race week is still held most summers.

The salt is also slowly shrinking. Some has been pumped away for industry, and racers worry that the crust is now thinner than it used to be.

The Great Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is different from Uyuni. It is a salt marsh that floods with seawater and rain during the monsoon, then dries out into a crust of white salt in winter. Under a full moon, the white ground glows so brightly that the area has become famous for its winter festival, the Rann Utsav.

Next door, the Little Rann is home to the Indian wild ass, found nowhere else in the world. Salt workers called Agariyas have harvested salt from shallow pans here for generations, evaporating brine pumped from underground, a process that turns on simple [[@evaporation-cooling|evaporation]].

Scientists have spotted what look like old salt deposits on Mars, left behind when its lakes dried up billions of years ago. On Earth, salt flats can trap tiny bubbles of ancient water inside their crystals. If life ever existed on Mars, some researchers think salty places like these are a good spot to look for traces of it.

That idea links Uyuni and the Rann to one of the biggest questions in science. And the salt in them shares a story with the salt in the ocean, explained in [[@why-sea-salty|why the sea is salty]].

text: "Stone forest" is a name for two quite different wonders. The first kind has no trees at all. It is a crowd of tall rock pillars, carved by rain until they stand like trunks in a wood. The most famous is Shilin, which simply means "stone forest", near Kunming in China.

The second kind was once a real forest. Its fallen trees were buried, and water full of minerals slowly turned them into stone. These petrified forests, as they are called, lie in places like Arizona in the USA and the Thar Desert near Jaisalmer in Rajasthan.

st.prompt: What carved the stone pillars of China's Shilin Stone Forest?

options.t: Rainwater slowly dissolving limestone
Ancient people with chisels

st.reveal: Rain picks up a little carbon dioxide and becomes a very weak acid. Over millions of years it seeped into cracks in thick limestone and widened them, leaving tall pillars standing between deep slots.

d.try: Stack a small tower of sugar cubes on a plate. Use a spoon or dropper to drip water slowly onto one spot at the top and watch channels and gaps form. Rain does the same thing to limestone, only millions of times more slowly.
myth: Petrified wood is just very old wood that has dried out and gone hard.
It is really stone. Minerals carried by water slowly filled and replaced the wood, cell by cell, until the log became rock that keeps the shape of rings and bark.

sec.t:
Limestone is made mostly of the shells and skeletons of sea creatures that piled up on old seabeds. It is tough, but it has one weakness. Rain mixes with a little carbon dioxide from the air and soil and becomes a very weak acid, about as weak as fizzy water. Limestone slowly dissolves in it.

Over millions of years, rain trickled into cracks and made them wider and deeper. The rock between the cracks was left standing. A landscape shaped this way is called [[karst|karst]], and the same process digs out huge [[@caves-form|caves]] underground. At Shilin, some pillars rise as high as a 10-storey building, and the forest spreads over about 350 square km.

Shilin's limestone formed on a seabed about 270 million years ago. Local Yi people tell the story of Ashima, a girl turned to stone, and point to one pillar said to be her. Walking paths wind through slots so narrow that two people cannot pass.

Madagascar has a sharper version called the Tsingy. Here the rain has cut the limestone into blades with edges like broken glass. Rangers clip visitors onto steel cables and rope bridges. Lemurs leap between the pinnacles, and some plants and animals live only there, which is one reason UNESCO protected it in 1990.

The Tsingy has a hidden basement too. Beneath the blades, water has carved caves and tunnels, and in places whole sections of roof have collapsed. That leaves deep green canyons with their own small forests, cut off from the rest of the island. Scientists exploring them keep finding species that nobody had described before, from tiny frogs to new kinds of lemur.

{{story:madagascar}}

In a petrified forest, the trees really were trees. About 225 million years ago, in what is now Arizona, rivers knocked down giant conifers and buried them in mud and volcanic ash. Groundwater rich in silica, the stuff of sand and glass, seeped in. Bit by bit, it filled every cell and replaced the wood.

The result is stone that keeps tree rings and bark, sometimes stained red, yellow and purple by iron and other minerals. Some logs at Petrified Forest National Park are longer than a school bus. US President Theodore Roosevelt protected the area in 1906, after visitors kept carting off pieces as souvenirs.

At Akal, about 17 km from Jaisalmer, lies a fossil wood park with tree trunks around 180 million years old. They grew when this hot, dry desert sat near a warm, swampy coast. The Geological Survey of India lists the site as a National Geological Monument. In Tamil Nadu, near Tiruvakkarai, more fossil trees lie scattered in the fields.

So the Thar was once a land of tall trees by the sea. That sounds impossible until you learn how the [[@thar-formed|Thar Desert formed]], and how [[@rocks-types|ordinary rocks]] can hold the shells of animals that died long before the first dinosaurs. And the strangest part? The same slow swap of minerals that turned these trunks to stone also turned dinosaur bones into [[@fossils-form|fossils]].

text: A landslide happens when rock, soil or mud on a slope suddenly moves downhill. [[@gravity-fall|Gravity]] is always pulling everything on a hillside down. Normally, [[@friction|friction]] and the strength of the ground hold it in place.

When something tips the balance, the slope gives way. Heavy rain is the most common trigger, especially in India's monsoon. Earthquakes, volcanoes, rivers eating away at the bottom of a slope, and people cutting into hillsides for [[@roads-built|roads]] and buildings can all set off landslides too.

st.prompt: Which of these usually makes a hillside most likely to slide?

options.t: Several days of very heavy rain
A week of strong sunshine
A cold, clear night

st.reveal: Rainwater soaks into the soil, making it heavier and filling the spaces between grains. That pushes the grains apart and reduces the friction holding them in place. Most landslides in India happen during the monsoon.

Some are sudden, but many give signs first, such as new cracks in the ground or walls, tilting trees or poles, or water bubbling up where it didn't before. Experts watch for these signs, and people in hilly areas are taught to report them.

sec.h: A tug of war on every slope
sec.t:
On every hillside, there is a quiet tug of war. Gravity pulls the soil and rock downhill. Friction between grains, the roots of plants, and the strength of the rock itself hold them back.

The steeper the slope, the harder gravity pulls. A gentle hill can stay put for thousands of years. A steep cliff of loose rock may only need a small push. Dry sand, for example, can't form a heap steeper than about 30 to 35 degrees before it starts to slide.

A little water can help soil stick together. That's why you can build a sandcastle with damp sand but not with dry sand. But too much water does the opposite.

When heavy rain soaks into a slope, it fills the tiny gaps between grains of soil. The water pushes the grains apart and makes the ground heavier. Friction drops, while the weight pressing downhill goes up. If a layer of clay or solid rock lies below, water can collect on top of it like a slippery sheet, and everything above slides off.

That's why so many landslides happen after days of rain, not just one shower. In India, most come during the [[@monsoon|monsoon]].

{{story:friction}}

Landslides come in many forms. In a rockfall, boulders break off a cliff and tumble down. In a slump, a chunk of hillside slides down along a curved surface, like a spoonful scooped from a pudding. In a mudflow or debris flow, soaked soil, rocks and trees rush downhill like a river, often following a valley. These can move faster than a car.

Some landslides are very slow, creeping a few centimetres a year. You can sometimes spot them by trees with curved trunks, fences out of line, or cracks in roads.

India's most landslide-prone regions are the Himalaya, which are young and still rising, and the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], where steep slopes meet some of the heaviest rain in the country. The Geological Survey of India has mapped which areas are most at risk.

In July 2024, after extremely heavy rain, huge landslides swept through villages in the Wayanad district of [[@kerala|Kerala]]. It was one of the worst landslide disasters in India's recent history, and rescue teams worked for weeks. Many experts pointed to the very heavy rain, the steep slopes and changes to the land as reasons it was so severe.

Strong [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]] shake slopes and can loosen thousands of landslides at once. In mountains, landslides often cause much of the damage after a big quake.

[[@volcano|Volcanoes]] can cause the biggest landslides of all. On 18 May 1980, an earthquake shook Mount St. Helens in Washington State. Its bulging north side collapsed in the largest landslide ever recorded, and the eruption burst out moments later.

People can make slopes safer. Planting trees and grasses helps, because roots bind the soil. Drains carry rainwater away before it soaks in. Walls and wire nets hold back loose rock along roads in the Himalaya and the Western Ghats.

Warning systems help too. Rain gauges and sensors on slopes can alert officials when the ground is getting dangerously wet. In the United States, the USGS works with weather forecasters to issue warnings when heavy rain could trigger debris flows, especially on hillsides recently burned by [[@people-firefighters-forest|wildfires]].

text: A [[mineral|mineral]] is a natural, solid substance with a fixed recipe of chemical elements, whose atoms are lined up in a repeating pattern called a [[crystal|crystal]]. Rocks are made of minerals, the way a fruit salad is made of different fruits.

Almost everything around you that isn't alive, or made from living things, came from minerals. The salt on your food is a mineral called halite. Glass is made mostly from quartz sand. The core of a pencil is graphite. Metals like iron, copper and [[@aluminium|aluminium]] come from minerals called ores, which are dug up and processed.
Even a smartphone holds dozens of different elements that started out inside rocks.

st.reveal: Talc is the softest mineral of all, number 1 on the Mohs hardness scale, and a fingernail (about 2.5) easily scratches it. Quartz is a 7 and diamond is a 10, the hardest natural mineral.

d.try: Gather a piece of blackboard chalk, a lump of rock salt or a big salt crystal, a pebble and a smooth piece of soapstone if you have one. Try to scratch each with your fingernail, then with a copper coin. Put them in order from softest to hardest, like a mini Mohs scale.
myth: Pencil lead is made of the metal lead, so chewing a pencil can poison you.
Pencils have never contained lead. The core is graphite and clay. The name stuck because people in the 1500s thought graphite was a kind of lead.

sec.h: In the kitchen and the bathroom

sec.t:
In the 1500s, people in Borrowdale, in northern England, found a deposit of a soft black mineral that left dark marks. They thought it was a kind of lead and called it "black lead". It was actually graphite, a form of pure carbon.

Shepherds used it to mark their sheep. Soon it was being cut into sticks and wrapped in wood. Today, pencil makers grind graphite and mix it with clay. More clay makes a harder, lighter pencil. More graphite makes a softer, darker one.

Graphite and diamond are both pure carbon. The only difference is how the atoms are arranged, yet one is soft enough to write with and the other is the hardest natural mineral on Earth.

A [[@smartphones|smartphone]] is a small mineral museum. The screen is a tough glass made from quartz sand. The tiny [[@semiconductors-india|chips]] are built on silicon, which also comes from quartz. Copper carries electricity through the wiring, and a little gold coats some contacts because it never rusts.

The [[@batteries-phones|battery]] needs lithium, and often cobalt and nickel. Magnets in the speakers and the buzzing motor use rare earth elements, which are not actually rare but are hard to separate.

Getting these minerals out of the ground has costs. Some mines damage forests and rivers. In some places, including parts of India's mica belt in Jharkhand, children have been found working in dangerous mines, a problem linked to [[@child-labour|child labour]] around the world. Mica is the glittery mineral that adds shimmer to some [[@art-materials|paints]] and cosmetics.

In 1812, a German scientist named Friedrich Mohs ranked ten minerals by hardness, from talc at 1 to diamond at 10. A mineral can scratch anything below it on the list. Your fingernail is about 2.5, a copper coin about 3 and steel about 5.5. Quartz, at 7, scratches glass, which is why sand blowing in the wind slowly frosts car windscreens.

Geologists still use the Mohs scale in the field. It is a quick way to tell one shiny grey rock from another with nothing but a coin.

text: A comet's tail is made of gas and dust that boil off its icy centre as it nears the Sun.

The centre, called the nucleus, is a lump of frozen water, frozen gases, dust and rock, usually a few kilometres wide. Far from the Sun it stays frozen and dark. As it swings closer, the Sun's heat turns some of its ice straight into gas, which drags dust out with it. This makes a glowing cloud around the nucleus and, often, two long tails. The tails can stretch for tens of millions of kilometres.

spots: A ball of ice, dust and rock, a few kilometres wide. A dirty snowball!
Dust pushed away by sunlight. It curves gently and looks yellowish-white.
Glowing gas blown straight away by the solar wind. It often looks blue.
Near the Sun, the ice turns to gas. Both tails point away from the Sun, even when the comet is leaving!

quiz.reveal: The tails are pushed by sunlight and by the solar wind, a stream of particles flowing out from the Sun. So they always point away from the Sun, whichever way the comet is moving. On the way out, the tail goes first.

sec.t:
Look closely at a bright comet and you may see two tails. The dust tail is broad and curved, and shines yellowish-white because the dust reflects sunlight. The gas tail is narrow and straight, and often glows blue.

They point slightly different ways because different things push them. Sunlight itself gently shoves the dust. The gas is blown straight back by the [[@solar-wind|solar wind]], a stream of charged particles that flows out from the [[@sun-what|Sun]]. Both always point away from the Sun.

Most comets spend almost all their time in the cold, dark outer solar system. Some come from the [[@kuiper-belt|Kuiper Belt]], the icy zone beyond [[@neptune-winds|Neptune]] where [[@pluto|Pluto]] lives. Others come from the Oort Cloud, a vast shell of icy bodies much farther out still.

Now and then, a nudge sends one falling inwards on a long, stretched orbit. Some comets return every few years. Others take thousands of years to come back. Old Indian texts call comets *dhumketu*, which means "smoke banner".

sec.h: The comet that came back on time

sec.t:
In 2014, the European Space Agency's Rosetta spacecraft reached a comet called 67P, after a ten-year journey. It released a small lander, Philae, which bounced twice before settling in a shadowy spot. Rosetta followed the comet for two years as it passed the Sun.

The comet turned out to be shaped like a rubber duck, with a surface darker than coal. Rosetta also measured its water. That water was different in one important way from the water in Earth's oceans. Scientists still argue about how much of [[@earth-age|Earth's water]] came from comets.

Comets are some of the oldest, least changed objects in the solar system. They formed about 4.6 billion years ago from the same cloud as the planets, and have stayed in the deep freeze ever since. Studying one is a little like opening a freezer that has been shut since the solar system was born.

Comets can also meet a dramatic end. In 1994, astronomers watched Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9, which [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]]'s gravity had torn into more than 20 pieces, crash into Jupiter one piece at a time. The impacts left dark scars bigger than Earth in Jupiter's clouds.

When a comet passes the Sun it leaves a trail of dust. When Earth later ploughs through that trail, we see a meteor shower of [[@shooting-stars|shooting stars]].

text: Fireflies make light by [[@bioluminescence|bioluminescence]], like deep-sea fish.
A firefly's light is "cold": nearly all the energy becomes light, not heat.

Inside the last few segments of a firefly's belly is a special light organ. There, a chemical called luciferin combines with oxygen, helped by an enzyme called luciferase. The reaction gives off light. By controlling how much air reaches the light organ, the firefly can switch its glow on and off in a fraction of a second.
Before [[@monsoon|the monsoon]], fireflies light up villages like Purushwadi in Maharashtra.

frames.cap: A firefly is a beetle with a glowing tail.

Each kind of firefly has its own flashing pattern, like a code, to find a partner.

sec.t:
Fireflies are not flies at all. They are beetles, with hard wing covers like a ladybird's. There are about 2,000 known species, living on every continent except Antarctica. Most fly in warm, damp places near forests, fields, streams and mangroves.

Not every firefly flashes as an adult. Some glow steadily, and some don't light up at all. But almost all firefly larvae, the young ones that live in soil and leaf litter, glow. Scientists think the glow first began as a warning. Many fireflies taste bitter to birds and lizards, and the light says "don't eat me".

In a few places, thousands of fireflies flash together, all at once, like strings of festival lights. Every June in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, in Tennessee, USA, one species does this in the forest at night. The show is so popular that the park runs a lottery for visitor passes.

In India, the village of Purushwadi in the Sahyadri hills of Maharashtra holds a firefly festival each May and June. Visitors come to see trees [[@blinking|blinking]] with thousands of fireflies on warm nights before the rains. Firefly watchers are encouraged to keep torches off and voices low, so the insects are not disturbed. Soon after, the [[@frogs-monsoon|monsoon]] arrives, along with the frogs.

An old-style [[@light-bulb|light bulb]] wasted about 90% of its energy as heat, which is why it got too hot to touch. A firefly's light organ gives off very little heat, because [[@how-glow-sticks|the chemical reaction turns energy straight into light]]. LED lights do something similar, which is why they stay cool.

Scientists also borrowed the firefly's tools. The gene for luciferase is used in labs around the world. When it is added to cells, they glow, letting researchers watch diseases and new medicines at work.

Many people say they see fewer fireflies than when they were young. Scientists who study them think the main reasons are the loss of wild, damp places, pesticides, and light from streetlamps and buildings. Bright lights at night can drown out firefly signals, so males and females fail to find each other. Keeping some gardens and fields [[@night-sky-dark|dark at night]], with long grass and leaf litter, gives fireflies a better chance.

text: A film is made in five big steps. First someone has an idea and writes a script. Then the team plans everything: actors, places, costumes, sets and money. Next comes the shoot, when cameras roll. After that, editors cut the footage together and add music, sound and effects. Finally the film is released in cinemas or online.
A big film can involve hundreds of people and take years. Even a short scene of two friends talking may need a day of filming, a dozen camera positions and lots of repeated takes.

st.prompt: In what order are the scenes of a film usually shot?

options.t: In whatever order saves time and money
From the first scene to the last
Last scene first, then backwards

st.reveal: Crews group together every scene at the same place, or with the same actors, and shoot them in a row. So an actor might film the ending on day three and the opening scene months later.

d.try: Make a flipbook. Draw a stick figure in the corner of 20 pages of an old notebook, moving its arm a tiny bit on each page. Flip the pages fast with your thumb. Films work the same way, only with 24 pictures every second.
myth: Films are shot in the same order you watch them.
Almost never. Shooting is planned around places, actors and weather. Editors put the scenes in order afterwards, which is why keeping track of details like a character's haircut is a real job on set.

sec.t:
Every film starts as words on a page. A screenplay lists what we see and hear, scene by scene. One page of script usually comes out to about one minute on screen, so a two-hour film's script is about 120 pages.

Many directors then draw a storyboard, a comic-strip version of the film showing each camera shot. It helps the whole team picture the scene before anyone builds a set or books an actor.

On shooting days, a crew might include camera operators, lighting technicians, sound recordists, make-up artists, costume designers and drivers. Each shot is repeated several times, called takes, until the director is happy.

Before each take, someone snaps a clapperboard in front of the camera. The sharp clap helps editors line up the sound, which is recorded separately, with the picture. The board also shows the scene and take number.

A person called the script supervisor watches tiny details. Was the glass half full or empty? Was the actor's collar up? Mistakes slip through anyway, and fans love spotting them.

Once filming ends, the editor may have hundreds of hours of footage for a two-hour film. Crews often shoot ten times more than they use, and sometimes far more. Choosing the best moments and putting them in order is where a film really takes shape. A single scene can change mood completely depending on which shots are used.

Then come [[@special-effects|special effects]], colour correction and sound. Many sounds you hear, such as footsteps, punches or a horse's hooves, are recorded later by Foley artists in a studio, using [[@behind-sound-effects|clever tricks]] like coconut shells for hooves. Finally a composer adds the music.

sec.h: Why it looks like it moves
sec.t:
A film is really a series of still pictures shown very fast, usually 24 every second. Your brain blends them into smooth motion. It is related to the tricks behind many [[@optical-illusions|optical illusions]].

The Lumière brothers held one of the first paid film shows in Paris in December 1895. Some viewers were startled by a train seemingly rushing towards them. Eighteen years later, in 1913, [[@dadasaheb-phalke|Dadasaheb Phalke]] released *Raja Harishchandra*, India's first full-length feature film. He did almost every job himself, and men played the female roles.

Today India makes films in more than 20 languages, from Hindi and Tamil to Telugu, Bengali, Malayalam, Kannada and Marathi. In most years it produces more feature films than any other country, far more than Hollywood.

Films also travel the other way. Many Indian films use American visual-effects studios, and many Hollywood films send their effects work to studios in Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad. When a superhero leaps off a building on screen, an artist in India may have made that jump look real. Or a trained performer may really have jumped, which is where the careful science of [[@behind-stunts|stunts]] comes in.

text: Not with just your eyes, and definitely not from the Moon. The Great Wall is very long but only about 5 to 8 m wide, and it's made of local earth and stone the same colour as the land around it. [[@china-today|China]]'s first astronaut, Yang Liwei, said after his flight in 2003 that he couldn't see it from orbit.

From the International [[@space-station|Space Station]], about 400 km up, astronauts can sometimes photograph it with a zoom lens, when the light and snow are just right. Big cities, highways and airports are much easier to spot, because they are wider and contrast with the land.
The idea that the wall can be seen from the Moon appeared in books before anyone had been to space at all.

st.prompt: Why is the Great Wall so hard to see from space?

options.t: It's underground
It's very long but narrow, and the same colour as the land
Clouds always cover it

st.reveal: The wall is thousands of kilometres long but only a few metres wide, like trying to see a human hair from more than 3 km away. It's also built from local stone and earth, so it blends in.

myth: The Great Wall of China is the only human-made thing you can see from the Moon.

From the Moon, about 3,84,000 km away, you can't make out any human-made structure with the naked eye. Even from the space station, about 400 km up, the wall is very hard to spot, while big cities and airports are easier.

sec.t:
The "Great Wall" is really many walls built and rebuilt over about 2,000 years, to protect Chinese states from raiders from the north. Together they stretch about 21,000 km, over half the way around Earth.

Around 221 BCE, the first emperor of a united China, Qin Shi Huang, joined up older walls. Later dynasties added their own. The famous stone and brick sections that tourists climb near [[@beijing|Beijing]] were mostly built by the Ming dynasty, between 1368 and 1644. The Ming wall alone runs for almost 9,000 km.

Ming-dynasty builders mixed cooked sticky rice into their lime mortar. In 2010, scientists found that a substance in the rice, called amylopectin, made the mortar stronger, more waterproof and better at resisting cracks. Some of it still holds today, after 500 years of rain and frost.

Builders used whatever was local. In the western deserts, where there was little stone, they packed layers of earth, sand and reeds into walls.

sec.h: Where the wall meets the sea
sec.t:
At its eastern end, near Shanhaiguan, the Ming wall runs right into the Bohai Sea, at a spot called Old Dragon's Head. In the far west, it ends at the fortress of Jiayuguan, on the edge of the Gobi Desert, a stop on the old [[@silk-road|Silk Road]].

Between them, the wall climbs steep mountain ridges that seem impossible to build on. Builders carried bricks up on their backs, or tied them to goats and donkeys.

The work was hard and dangerous. Soldiers, farmers and prisoners were forced to build it, and many died. Chinese folk tales remember this, such as the story of Meng Jiangnu, whose tears for her husband, lost while building the wall, were said to make part of it collapse.

Millions of tourists visit each year, especially at Badaling and Mutianyu near Beijing. Away from these sections, much of the wall is crumbling. A survey reported in 2015 that about a third of the Ming wall had disappeared, worn by weather or taken by villagers for building stone. It became a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1987, and repair work goes on.

text: The Barefoot College is an organisation in Tilonia, a village in Rajasthan, that trains rural people with little or no schooling to do skilled jobs. Its students learn to be solar engineers, water engineers, teachers, health workers and builders. Bunker Roy, a social worker, started it in 1972 as the Social Work and Research Centre.

The name comes from an idea. The college believes knowledge from experience, the kind held by village people who often walk barefoot, matters as much as degrees. Its best-known project trains grandmothers from India and dozens of other countries to build and repair solar lighting systems.

st.prompt: Women from many countries train together at Barefoot College, often with no shared language. How do they learn?

options.t: With colour-coded parts, gestures and lots of hands-on practice
By reading thick English textbooks
Through long lectures with translators for every language

st.reveal: Trainers use colours, pictures and sign language, and the women learn by building circuits and lamps again and again. Many cannot read, which matters far less than steady hands and practice.

d.try: On a sunny day, fill two identical cups with the same amount of water. Wrap one in black paper and one in white paper and leave them in the sun for an hour. Feel which is warmer. Dark surfaces soak up more sunlight, which is why solar water heaters are painted black.
myth: Solar power only works in rich countries or at giant power plants.
Small solar kits with one panel, a battery and a few lamps can light a home anywhere sunny. In villages far from the power grid, they often arrive before electricity cables do.

sec.t:
The college chose older women on purpose. Young men who learned a skill often left their villages for jobs in cities. Grandmothers usually stayed, and their neighbours already trusted them.

The women come to Tilonia for about six months. Many cannot read and do not share a language with each other. Trainers use colour-coded wires and parts, hand signals and repeated practice. By the end, the women can put together [[@solar-panels|solar panels]], batteries, charge controllers and lamps, and fix them when they break. Women have come from Africa, Latin America, the Pacific and Asia, with India's government paying for many of them.

When the women go home, they set up solar systems in houses that have never had electricity. A child who had to stop reading at sunset can study at night. Families stop buying kerosene, whose smoke harms lungs and whose flames can start fires.

People in the village pay a small monthly fee to the solar engineer for repairs. So the grandmother earns a living, and a broken lamp gets fixed instead of thrown away. In some villages, she becomes the most important technical expert for many kilometres around, the person people call when anything electrical stops working.

The college campus in Tilonia was designed with help from a professional architect, but villagers built it themselves using local stone, mud and simple methods. In 2001, the buildings won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture, one of the world's best-known prizes for architecture.

Water is precious in the Thar region. The roofs are built to collect rain and send it into large underground tanks, a technique called [[@rainwater-harvesting|rainwater harvesting]]. A single good monsoon can fill them with enough water to last the dry months.

To spread ideas about health, water and rights, the college uses [[@puppetry|puppetry]], songs and street plays. Puppets made from recycled paper can say things a stranger cannot, and a crowd will gather to watch them where nobody would come to a lecture.

The college has its critics. Some ask how well its solar systems keep working years after the training, when spare parts are far away, and whether its methods can grow without losing their spirit. Supporters point to the grandmothers who still keep their villages lit. Their stories have travelled widely, and the same sunshine that powers a single lamp in Tilonia now powers giant solar parks across [[@solar-india|India]].

text: Children have learned from adults for as long as there have been people, by watching, listening and helping. But schools, special places where [[@jobs-teacher|a teacher]] instructs a group of students, began about 4,000 to 5,000 years ago, soon after writing was invented.

For thousands of years, only a small number of children went to school, mostly boys from rich or priestly families. The idea that every child should go to school, paid for by the government, is surprisingly recent. It spread in the 1700s and 1800s, and in many countries, including India, it became law only in the last hundred years.

st.prompt: In the United States, why do schools have a long summer holiday?

options.t: Mostly because city schools were too hot and families liked summer breaks
Because children were needed on farms in summer
Because teachers asked to be paid less

st.reveal: Historians say farm children were most needed in spring for planting and autumn for harvest, not in summer. The long summer break was shaped by city reformers who worried about hot, stuffy classrooms and by families who left cities in summer.

d.try: Ask your grandparents or older relatives what school was like for them. How did they get there? What did they write on? What were the punishments? Write down their answers and compare them with your own school day.
myth: The long summer holiday exists because children used to be needed on farms.

Farm work was busiest at planting and harvest time, in spring and autumn. Historians trace the American summer break mainly to city school reformers in the 1800s, who standardised calendars and avoided teaching in the summer heat.
facts: First US state with compulsory schooling

sec.t:
After [[@writing-began|writing]] was invented in Mesopotamia, scribes were needed to keep records. In schools that the Sumerians called *edubba*, or "tablet houses", boys learned to press wedge-shaped signs into wet clay. They copied lists of words, solved maths problems and practised writing contracts. Archaeologists have found their practice tablets, complete with mistakes and corrections.

[[@ancient-egypt|Ancient Egypt]], China and Greece had schools too, mostly for training scribes, officials and priests.

In 1763, the king of Prussia, in what is now Germany, ordered that children should attend school. In the United States, Massachusetts passed the first state law making school attendance compulsory in 1852. By 1918, every US state had such a law.

In India, schools for girls and for children of oppressed castes were rare until reformers pushed for them. In 1848, [[@jyotirao-phule|Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule]] opened a girls' school in [[@pune|Pune]]. Savitribai became one of India's first women teachers, despite fierce opposition.

When India became independent in 1947, most Indians could not read. At the 1951 [[@census|census]], only about 18% were literate. Governments built schools across the country, and the [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]] scheme encouraged poor families to send children to class. In 2009, the Right to Education Act made free schooling a right for every child aged 6 to 14, as part of the wider [[@rights-kids|rights of children]]. By 2011, literacy had reached about 74%.

Classrooms changed too. For centuries, students wrote on slates with chalk, because paper was expensive. Indian children practised letters on wooden boards called *takhtis*, or traced them in sand. Ballpoint pens became common only after the Second World War, and computers reached most classrooms only in recent decades.

Around the world, about 27 crore children and young people were out of school in 2025, according to UNESCO. War, poverty, distance and the need to work keep many at home, and girls are often the first to be kept back. Ideas about what school should look like keep changing too, as you can see in [[@schools-world|schools around the world]].

text: February has 28 days because of the ancient Roman calendar. The Romans added it late, made it the last month of their year, and gave it the leftover days. Later rulers fixed the calendar to match the Sun, but they kept February short and simply added a spare day to it every few years.
So the odd month you live with today is a patch on top of a patch, more than 2,000 years old.

st.prompt: Will the year 2100 be a leap year?

options.t: No, because it is a century year not divisible by 400
Yes, because it divides by 4
Yes, every year ending in 00 is a leap year

st.reveal: Under the Gregorian rule, century years only get a leap day if they divide by 400. So 2000 was a leap year, but 2100 will not be.

d.try: Make a fist and count the months across your knuckles and the dips between them, starting with January on the first knuckle. Months on knuckles have 31 days and months in the dips have fewer. When you reach July on the last knuckle, start again on the first knuckle with August.
myth: Emperor Augustus stole a day from February so his month, August, would be as long as July.
There is no Roman evidence for this. The story was told by a writer in the Middle Ages, more than a thousand years later. August already had 31 days before Augustus renamed it.

Days skipped in Britain and its colonies

sec.h: A year with a hole in it
sec.t:
Roman writers said their earliest calendar had just ten months, starting in March and ending in December. That is why September, October, November and December are named after the Latin for seven, eight, nine and ten. Winter, when there was little farm work, was simply not counted.

According to tradition, King Numa Pompilius added January and February around 700 BCE. Romans considered even numbers unlucky, so most months got 29 or 31 days. But twelve odd numbers can't add up to an odd total like 355. One month had to be even, and February, a month for remembering the dead, got 28.

Caesar's year averaged 365.25 days. That is about 11 minutes too long. Eleven minutes sounds like nothing, but over centuries it added up. By the 1500s the calendar was about ten days out of step with the Sun.

In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII made a new rule. Century years, like 1700 or 1900, would skip their leap day unless they divide by 400. Catholic countries jumped ahead ten days at once. Britain waited until 1752, by which time it needed to skip 11 days. Its colonies, including the thirteen American colonies and the British-ruled parts of India, changed with it. That is why George Washington's birthday moved from 11 February to 22 February.

Because the month lengths follow no neat pattern, people invented tricks to remember them. English-speaking children learn an old rhyme that begins "Thirty days hath September, April, June and November". It goes back at least to the 1500s in England.

Another trick uses your knuckles. Make a fist and count the months across the bumps and the dips. Every month that lands on a bump has 31 days. July and August both land on bumps, side by side, because two 31-day months sit next to each other in the middle of the year. February sits in a dip, as it has for more than 2,000 years.

The Gregorian year averages 365.2425 days. The real year is 365.2422. The gap is so small that the calendar will only be about one day off after roughly 3,000 years.

Many people use more than one calendar. India's national calendar, adopted in 1957, is based on the Saka era, and its months start in March. Most traditional [[@indian-calendars|Indian calendars]], like the Jewish and Chinese ones, follow both the Moon and the Sun. The Islamic calendar follows the Moon alone. That is why Diwali moves around a little each year, while Eid slides about 11 days earlier every year and travels right through the seasons.

text: The first units came from things people always had with them: their bodies. A foot was the length of a foot. A cubit, used in [[@ancient-egypt|ancient Egypt]] and India, was the length of a forearm. A pace was a step. These were handy, but everyone's body is different, so different towns and kingdoms ended up with different units.

Over centuries, rulers tried to fix standard sizes so that trade would be fair. Britain's system of inches, feet, yards and miles spread with its empire. In the 1790s, France invented the metric system, based on tens and on the size of the Earth. Most of the world has since switched to metric. The United States is the biggest country that still mainly uses the older units in daily life.

st.prompt: Where does the name "foot" for a unit of length come from?

options.t: The length of a person's foot
The width of a horse's hoof
The height of a step on a staircase

st.reveal: Many old units came from the human body, because everyone always had one handy. A foot was roughly a man's foot. A cubit was the length from the elbow to the fingertip, and a hand, still used to measure horses, was the width of a palm.

d.try: Measure the length of a table using your hand span, then ask a grown-up to measure it with theirs. You'll get different answers. Now measure it with a ruler. This is the problem that standard units were invented to solve.
myth: The United States doesn't use the metric system at all.

Americans use miles, pounds and feet in daily life, but science, medicine and the military in the US use metric units. Soft drinks are sold in 2-litre bottles, and even the inch is legally defined in centimetres.

sec.t:
A hand is about the width of a palm, roughly 10 cm. It is still used to measure the height of horses. A yard was said to be the distance from an English king's nose to his outstretched thumb, though that story may be a legend.

[[@measurement-india|India had its own body units]]. An *angula* was the width of a finger. A *hasta*, or *hath*, was the length from elbow to fingertip, like a cubit. Builders of temples used these units, and old texts on architecture describe buildings in them.

The problem with bodies is obvious. A tall trader buying cloth by the arm's length would get more than a short one.

By the 1700s, France alone had hundreds of different units, and the same name could mean different sizes in different towns. After the [[@french-revolution|French Revolution]], scientists created the [[@metric-system|metric system]]. Everything was based on tens, so you could change centimetres to metres just by moving a decimal point.

India adopted the metric system by a law passed in 1956, and switched over during the following years. The rupee had already become decimal, with 100 paise instead of 16 annas. Kilograms replaced seers in markets, and kilometres replaced miles on road signs.

In September 1999, NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter reached Mars after a ten-month journey. Then it vanished. An investigation found that one engineering team's software reported the push of its small thrusters in pound units. Another team's software expected newton units, which are metric.

Each small mistake added up. The spacecraft flew much too close to Mars and was destroyed or skipped off into space. It was an expensive lesson in checking units. Today's [[@mars-rovers|Mars rovers]] are planned entirely in metric.

In the US, rulers often show inches on one edge and centimetres on the other. Since 1959, an inch has been defined as exactly 2.54 centimetres, so the old units are now officially measured in metric. In India, people may still talk about a room in square feet or their height in feet and inches, while buying vegetables in kilograms. The two systems still live side by side.

text: Every sport looks strange if you have never seen it. Cricket can last five days and still end in a draw, which amazes many Americans. American football stops every few seconds, which baffles many Indians. But some sports are odd by any standard.

There is chess boxing, where brains and fists take turns. There is cheese rolling, wife carrying, bog snorkelling and underwater hockey. India has its own surprises, like buffalo racing through muddy rice fields. Most weird sports started as a joke, a village festival or a bet, and then refused to die.

Only by winning the chess game
By scoring the most punches overall

st.reveal: You can win on the board or in the ring. A strong boxer may try to tire out a chess player, while a strong chess player hopes to checkmate before the next boxing round.

myth: The Olympics have only ever had serious, ordinary sports.
Tug of war was an Olympic sport from 1900 to 1920, and early Games also had live pigeon shooting and a swimming obstacle race. Sports come and go as tastes change.

sec.t:
Chess boxing began as an idea in a French comic book. In 2003, a Dutch artist organised the first real match. Players alternate short rounds of chess and boxing, up to eleven rounds in all. You win by checkmate, by knockout, or if your opponent runs out of time on the chess clock.

The hard part is thinking clearly with your heart pounding. Try planning five moves ahead a minute after being punched. Fans say it is the perfect test of body and mind. Most top [[@chess-champions|chess players]] are happy to skip it.

In Finland, the Wife Carrying World Championships began in 1992. A man carries his partner, often upside down on his back, through an obstacle course with a water pit. In Wales, bog snorkellers swim two lengths of a muddy trench in a peat bog, using flippers but no normal swimming strokes.

Underwater hockey was invented in England in 1954 by divers who wanted to keep fit in winter. Players wear snorkels and push a heavy puck along the bottom of a pool with short sticks, holding their breath for each dive.

sec.h: Kicking a ball over a net
sec.t:
Sepak takraw looks like volleyball, but players may not use their hands. They kick a woven ball over a net, often with bicycle kicks in mid-air. It is hugely popular in Thailand, Malaysia and other parts of South-East Asia and has been part of the Asian Games since 1990. India won its first medal in the sport, a bronze, in 2018.

In the USA, a version of quidditch from the [[@harry-potter-effect|Harry Potter]] books began at a college in Vermont in 2005. Players run with broomsticks between their legs. It is now called quadball.

In coastal Karnataka, Kambala racers sprint through flooded rice fields beside pairs of buffaloes, holding the reins. The water splashes as high as their heads. In 2020, one racer's time made headlines when people compared it to Usain Bolt's, though the two races cannot really be compared.

Kambala is centuries old and tied to the farming year, held after the harvest in the cool months. Then there is [[@sport-mallakhamb|mallakhamb]], where gymnasts climb, twist and balance on a wooden pole, or even on a hanging rope. And weird sports are nothing new. The [[@oddity-ancient-olympics-weird|ancient Olympics]] had an event where athletes raced in full armour.

text: Air is a mixture of gases, about 21% oxygen. That share stays the same whether you are on Marine Drive in Mumbai or on top of Everest. What changes is how tightly the air is packed. Near the sea, the weight of all the air above squeezes it together. Climb higher and there is less air above you, so the air is thinner.

Thin air means each breath holds fewer molecules of oxygen. Your lungs have to work harder, your heart beats faster, and you may get a headache. On the summit of Everest, at 8,849 metres, the [[pressure|air pressure]] is only about a third of what it is at sea level.

st.prompt: High on a mountain, what is different about the air?

options.t: It is thinner, so each breath holds fewer oxygen molecules
It contains a smaller percentage of oxygen
It is full of extra carbon dioxide

st.reveal: The air is still about 21% oxygen, just as at sea level. But there is less air pressing down from above, so the air is spread out. Each lungful simply carries fewer molecules of everything, oxygen included.

d.try: On a family trip up a hill road, or on a flight, ask an adult to bring a sealed packet of chips. Look at it at the bottom and again at the top. The packet puffs up because the air outside is pressing on it less hard than the air sealed inside.
myth: There is less oxygen in mountain air because oxygen is heavy and sinks.

The mix of gases is almost the same at sea level and on a mountain top. What changes is the air pressure. Thinner air means fewer oxygen molecules in each breath, even though the percentage stays about 21%.

sec.t:
Oxygen gets into your body through tiny air sacs in your [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]], called [[alveoli|alveoli]]. From there it jumps into red blood cells, where a protein called [[haemoglobin|haemoglobin]] carries it around. When the air is thin, less oxygen crosses over with each breath.

Your body reacts within minutes. You breathe faster and deeper. Your heart speeds up to push blood around more quickly. Stairs feel like a hill. Leh, in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], sits about 3,500 metres up. Its airport is higher than any peak in the Western Ghats or the Appalachians. Tourists who fly in from Delhi are told to rest for a whole day before doing anything, and hotels often keep oxygen cylinders handy.

Over days and weeks, the body adjusts. This is called acclimatisation. The kidneys release a hormone that tells bone marrow to make more red blood cells, so the blood can carry more oxygen. Breathing settles into a new, faster pattern.

That is why athletes sometimes train at height, in places such as Ooty or the mountains of Colorado. Denver, in the USA, calls itself the Mile High City because it sits about 1,600 metres (one mile) up, and visiting sports teams often complain of puffing harder than usual.

Some people have lived high up for thousands of years. Tibetans, Sherpas in Nepal, and people in the Andes of South America all cope with thin air better than most lowlanders. Their bodies have adapted in different ways. Many Tibetans have a version of a gene called EPAS1 that stops their blood from becoming too thick. Scientists traced it to the Denisovans, an extinct group of ancient humans.

Studies in the Andes found that children who grow up in the high Andes, around La Paz in Bolivia, tend to develop bigger chests and lungs than children raised by the sea.

Animals manage too. The [[@bar-headed-goose|bar-headed goose]] flies over the Himalaya on migration, and yaks have huge lungs and hearts.

Above about 8,000 metres, the air is so thin that the body slowly runs down, however well it has adjusted. Climbers call it the death zone. Most people who climb Everest breathe bottled oxygen there. Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary used it on the [[@everest-first|first ascent]] in 1953. In 1978, Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler reached the summit without it, something many doctors had thought impossible.

text: Tears do three jobs. All the time, your eyes make a thin film of tears that keeps them wet, clean and smooth, so you can see clearly. When dust, smoke or onion fumes get in, your eyes make a flood of tears to wash them out. And when you feel very sad, very happy, hurt or moved, you may cry emotional tears.
Tears are made by the lacrimal glands, which sit under the bone above the outer corner of each eye. Every [[@blinking|blink]] spreads the tears across the eye like a windscreen wiper.
Usually tears drain away into your nose. When you cry, the glands make more than the drains can handle, so tears spill over onto your cheeks.

options.t: Down tiny tubes into your nose
They dry up on the surface of your eye
Back into the glands that made them

st.reveal: A little evaporates, but most tears drain through two tiny holes at the inner corner of each eye and down a tube into your nose. That is why crying gives you a runny nose.

National Eye Institute (USA), dry eye.
n.certNote: Scientists understand how tears are made and drained. Why humans cry when they feel strong emotions is still debated, and claims that crying flushes out stress chemicals have weak evidence.

d.try: Look closely in a mirror at the inner corner of your lower eyelid, near your nose. You should see a tiny dot, like a pinprick. That is a tear drain, called a punctum. There is another on the upper lid. Don't poke them, just look.
myth: Crying gets rid of stress chemicals, so you always feel better afterwards.

Some people do feel better after a cry, especially if someone comforts them. But studies have not shown that tears carry away enough stress chemicals to matter, and some people feel worse after crying.

sec.h: A thin shield for your eyes
sec.t:
The tear film on your eye is thinner than a sheet of paper, but it has three layers. An oily outer layer stops it drying out. A watery middle layer carries salt, oxygen and germ-fighting proteins. A sticky inner layer helps the tears cling to the eye.

Without this film your eyes would feel gritty and sore, and you couldn't [[@eyes-see|see]] well. People with dry eyes often use eye drops, a kind of artificial tears.

If a speck of dust lands in your eye, nerves in the eye send a message to your brain. The brain tells the lacrimal glands to make lots of tears fast. These are reflex tears. They rinse the speck away.

Cutting an [[@onions-tears|onion]] works the same way. When you slice it, the onion releases a gas that drifts up and irritates the nerves on the surface of your eye. Your eyes sting, and reflex tears rush in to wash it out.

Emotional tears are the puzzle. Humans cry when they are sad, but also when they are proud, relieved or laughing hard. Many animals make tears to clean their eyes, but scientists know of no other animal that clearly cries because of its feelings.

So why do we do it? One popular idea is that tears are a signal. They show others that we are upset or need help, without words. Babies start this way: crying brings an adult running. Later in life, a friend's tears can make us want to comfort them, a sign of [[@empathy|empathy]].

Researchers like Ad Vingerhoets in the Netherlands, who has studied crying for decades, think this social signal is the main reason we evolved to weep. Other ideas are still being tested.

{{story:emotions}}

Newborn babies cry a lot, but often without tears. Their tear glands are still developing, so emotional tears usually appear only after a few weeks, sometimes a couple of months. Their eyes still make enough basal tears to stay moist.

As children grow, they usually cry less often. Adults cry too, men as well as women, though people in some families and cultures are taught to hide it.

People say someone is crying "crocodile tears" when they pretend to be sad. The phrase comes from an old belief that crocodiles weep while eating their prey.

Oddly, it's partly true. In 2007 scientists filmed [[@crocodiles-alligators|caimans and alligators]] eating, and several of them did shed tears. The tears were probably caused by the hissing and huffing as the animals ate, which pushed air through their sinuses and squeezed their tear glands. The tears had nothing to do with sorrow.

So whether you are chopping onions, standing in the wind or watching a sad film, your tears are doing a job. If your eyes are often sore, red or watery for no clear reason, it is worth telling a parent or seeing a doctor.

text: Dandruff is flakes of dead skin falling from the scalp. Everyone sheds skin, all over the body, every day. Usually the bits are too tiny to notice. With dandruff, the scalp sheds faster, and the dead cells clump into white or yellowish flakes that land on shoulders and collars.

The main cause is a yeast called *Malassezia*, a microscopic [[fungus|fungus]] that lives on nearly everyone's skin. It feeds on the oil in hair follicles. As it eats, it leaves behind substances that irritate some people's skin. Their scalp responds by making new skin cells too fast, and flakes pile up.

st.prompt: What is a dandruff flake mostly made of?

options.t: Clumps of dead skin cells stuck together with oil
Dried shampoo
Tiny bits of broken hair

st.reveal: Your scalp sheds dead skin all the time, but usually in pieces too small to see. With dandruff, the skin renews faster, and dead cells clump together with oil into flakes big enough to spot on a dark shirt.

Britannica, Dandruff.

d.try: See how yeast loves food. With a grown-up, put a spoon of dried yeast in two cups of warm water, adding a spoon of sugar to one cup only. After 15 minutes, compare the foam. The scalp yeast that causes dandruff works the same way, but its favourite food is the oil from your skin.
myth: Dandruff happens because you don't wash your hair, or because your scalp is too dry.

Dandruff is mainly caused by a yeast that feeds on scalp oil, not by being dirty. Washing helps keep flakes under control, but clean people get dandruff too. A dry, flaky scalp in winter is a different, milder problem.

sec.t:
*Malassezia* is a distant relative of the yeast used in making bread. It is so small that thousands could sit on the head of a pin. It has lived on human skin for so long that it can no longer make some of the fats it needs. It has to get them from us.

So it heads for places with plenty of oil: the scalp, the face, the chest and behind the ears. It breaks down the oil into smaller pieces. One of them, oleic acid, can irritate the skin.

In most people, the scalp doesn't mind. In people with dandruff, it reacts with mild redness and itching, and the skin renews in a rush.

Young children rarely have dandruff, because their scalps make little oil. During [[@puberty-basics|puberty]], hormones switch on the oil glands. The yeast suddenly has a feast, and dandruff often appears for the first time.

Babies sometimes get a crusty, yellowish scalp called cradle cap, which is linked to the same yeast. It is harmless and usually clears up on its own.

Dandruff often gets worse in cold, dry winters and better in summer sunshine. Stress, tiredness and illness can make it flare up. Not washing hair for a long time lets oil and flakes build up, though washing more doesn't always cure it.

Some people notice more flakes after using hair gels or sprays, which can leave a crust on the scalp that looks similar.

It is not contagious. You can't catch dandruff by sharing a comb or sitting next to someone, because almost everyone already carries the yeast.

Special anti-dandruff shampoos contain ingredients that slow down the yeast or calm the skin. Common ones are zinc pyrithione, ketoconazole and selenium sulfide. They usually work best if left on the scalp for a few minutes before rinsing.

In India, many families also use traditional remedies such as coconut oil, neem or curd. Some people find them soothing, but there is less scientific evidence that they work. If the scalp gets very red, painful or itchy, or flakes spread to the face, it is worth talking to a parent or a doctor.

Dandruff is only one way your body loses old skin. Over a year, those tiny flakes add up to a surprising pile. Much of it ends up in household dust. There it becomes dinner for tiny creatures you never see: the [[@gross-dust-mites|dust mites]] living in your pillow.

text: Hormones are chemical messengers. They are made in small organs called [[gland|glands]], released into the blood, and carried all around the body. Only cells with the right [[receptor|receptors]] respond to each hormone, a bit like a key that fits only certain locks.

Nerves send messages fast, in a fraction of a second. Hormones are slower but longer-lasting. They control things that unfold over minutes, hours or years: how fast you grow, when you feel sleepy, how much sugar is in your blood, and the changes of [[@puberty-basics|puberty]].

st.prompt: India adds a tiny amount of one element to most table salt to help a hormone-making gland work properly. Which one?

options.t: Iodine
Iron
Calcium

st.reveal: The thyroid gland in your neck needs iodine to make its hormones. Without enough, it can swell into a lump called a goitre. Iodised salt has made goitre far less common in India and many other countries.

The Nobel Prize, Physiology or Medicine 1923 (Banting and Macleod, discovery of insulin).

d.try: Check the salt packet in your kitchen. Look for the word "iodised" or "iodized" and the amount of iodine listed. Then look up on a map where the thyroid gland sits in the body and find the spot on your own neck, just below the voice box.
myth: Hormones only matter when you hit puberty.
Hormones work in your body from before birth to old age. They control growth, sleep, hunger, blood sugar, body temperature and how you react to a fright, every single day.
facts: a chemical messenger carried in the blood
glands such as the pituitary, thyroid, adrenals and pancreas
1905, from a Greek word meaning "to set in motion"

sec.t:
Think of nerves as phone calls and hormones as letters posted to many addresses at once. A single hormone released into the blood can reach every organ within about a minute.

The main glands include the pituitary, a gland the size of a pea at the base of the brain, which tells many other glands what to do. The thyroid in your neck sets how fast your body burns energy. The adrenal glands sit on top of your kidneys. The pancreas, tucked behind your stomach, controls blood sugar. Together, these glands are called the endocrine system.

When you get a sudden scare, your adrenal glands release [[adrenaline|adrenaline]]. Within seconds your heart beats faster, you breathe quicker and your muscles get ready to act. This is often called the "fight or flight" response, and [[@stress|stress]] can switch it on too.

As evening falls and light fades, a tiny gland in the brain releases melatonin, which helps make you sleepy. Bright screens late at night can delay it. Then, during deep sleep, the pituitary releases growth hormone in bursts. That is one reason [[@sleep-why|sleep]] matters so much for growing children.

Your thyroid needs iodine, an element found in seafood and in soil, to make its hormones. In places where soil is low in iodine, including large areas along the Himalaya and in parts of the USA's Great Lakes region, many people once developed goitre, a swollen thyroid.

The USA began adding iodine to table salt in 1924. India started a national goitre control programme in 1962 and later moved towards iodising almost all edible salt. It is one of the simplest health measures ever invented, and it works quietly in kitchens across both countries.

In 1902, two British scientists, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling, discovered that the gut releases a chemical into the blood that tells the pancreas to start working. In 1905, Starling named such chemicals hormones, from a Greek word meaning "to set in motion". Scientists now know of more than 50 different hormones in the human body, and they are still finding new ones.

text: A fingerprint sensor reads the pattern of ridges on your fingertip and checks it against one you saved earlier. It doesn't look at the whole swirl the way you would. It hunts for small details called minutiae: the places where a ridge ends, or splits into two like a fork in a road.

When you first set up the phone, it records the positions of these points over many touches and saves them as a coded template. Each later touch is compared with that template. If enough points line up, the phone opens. All of this happens in a fraction of a second.

st.prompt: Most phone fingerprint sensors don't take a photo of your finger. What do capacitive sensors measure instead?

options.t: Tiny differences in electric charge where ridges touch and valleys don't
The heat coming from your blood
The smell of your skin

st.reveal: A capacitive sensor is a grid of thousands of tiny electrical cells. Ridges of skin touch the surface and change the charge in the cells below them, while the valleys between ridges leave small air gaps. The pattern of changes draws your print.

d.try: Rub a soft pencil on paper until you have a dark patch, press a fingertip on it, then press the finger onto clear sticky tape and stick the tape on white paper. Use a magnifying glass to find places where a ridge stops or splits in two. Compare prints from different family members.
myth: Your phone stores a photo of your fingerprint that hackers could steal and print.

Most phones turn the scan into a coded list of key points and keep it locked in a separate secure part of the chip. The original image isn't kept, and the template can't easily be turned back into a picture.

all ten fingerprints, both irises and a photo

sec.h: Three ways to read a ridge
sec.t:
**Optical sensors** take a picture. A light shines on your finger and a tiny camera captures the bright and dark lines. Many phones with sensors under the screen use this kind, lighting the finger with the display itself.

**Capacitive sensors** are a grid of thousands of tiny electrical cells. Your skin conducts a little [[@electricity-made|electricity]]. Where a ridge touches the surface, it changes the charge in the cell beneath it. Where there's a valley, a thin layer of air sits in between. The sensor turns these differences into a map.

**Ultrasonic sensors** send out pulses of very high-pitched [[@sound-travel|sound]] that people can't hear. The [[@echoes|echoes]] bounce back differently from ridges and valleys, building a 3D picture, even through a layer of glass.

{{story:fingerprints}}

[[@fingerprints|Fingerprints]] form [[@baby-development|before birth]] and stay the same all your life, growing larger but keeping the same pattern. Even [[@twins|identical twins]], who share the same genes, have different prints, because the ridges are shaped by tiny differences in how each baby grew and pressed against its surroundings in the womb.

Police have used fingerprints to identify people for more than a hundred years. In the 1890s in Bengal, two Indian police officers, Azizul Haque and Hem Chandra Bose, helped develop a way of sorting prints into groups so they could be found quickly. It became known as the Henry system, after their British boss.

Phones keep the fingerprint template in a walled-off part of the processor, often called a secure enclave. Apps can't read it. They only get a "yes" or "no" answer. The template also never needs to leave the phone.

Fingerprints are a kind of [[biometric|biometric]] key: something you are, rather than something you know, like a [[@passwords|password]]. That makes them convenient, but you can't change them if they're ever copied. For this reason, phones still ask for a passcode after a restart.

India's [[@aadhaar|Aadhaar]] system holds the fingerprints and iris scans of more than 130 crore people. When someone collects rations or opens a bank account, a small scanner checks their finger against the national record. This lets people prove who they are without paper documents.

It doesn't always work smoothly. Farm workers, labourers and older people can have worn or cracked fingertips that scanners struggle to read, which is why iris scans and one-time codes are used as backups.

Researchers have shown that some sensors can be tricked by fake fingers made of gelatin or glue moulded from a real print. Newer sensors try to check that the finger is alive, for example by looking at how skin flexes. No lock is perfect, but for most people a fingerprint is far harder to steal than a four-digit code someone sees over your shoulder.

text: Most experts expect that by 2050, much more of our energy will come from the Sun and the wind, stored in giant batteries and carried along much bigger power grids. Hydropower, nuclear power and perhaps hydrogen will fill the gaps. Coal and oil will probably still be used, but far less than today.

That shift has already begun. In 2025, renewable sources made 33.8% of the world's electricity, just ahead of coal at 33.0%, according to the energy research group Ember. Solar power grew so fast that it passed wind for the first time. How far it goes by 2050 depends on money, politics and technology, and forecasts disagree. That is why this article is marked mixed.

st.prompt: In 2025, which source made more of the world's electricity than ever before and passed wind power for the first time?

options.t: Solar power
Nuclear power
Coal

st.reveal: Solar generation jumped by about 30% in 2025 and passed wind globally for the first time, according to the energy think tank Ember. Together, all renewables made slightly more electricity than coal.

n.certNote: Nobody can be sure what 2050 will look like. Forecasts from energy agencies disagree, especially about how fast coal and oil will fall and whether new technologies like fusion will be ready.

That is a real challenge, but it is being solved with batteries, pumped water storage, power lines that move electricity between regions, and backup sources like hydro and nuclear. Some countries already get most of their electricity from renewables on many days.

sec.t:
The Sun sets and the wind drops, but people still want lights on at 9 pm. So the big puzzle of 2050 is storage. [[@batteries-future|Batteries]] are getting cheaper every year, and power companies now build battery farms the size of football grounds.

Another trick is pumped hydro. When electricity is cheap, pumps push water uphill into a lake. When it is needed, the water rushes down through turbines. It is like a giant rechargeable battery made of water and mountains.

[[@wind-turbines|Wind turbines]] are getting taller and their blades longer. Some offshore blades are longer than a football field, catching steadier winds out at sea. Dams already give a large share of power in countries like Norway and Brazil, as well as parts of the Himalaya.

Nuclear power, which splits atoms, makes no smoke and runs day and night. Some countries, including India, plan to build more reactors. Others are closing them because of cost and worries about waste. Scientists honestly disagree on how big nuclear's part should be.

Some technologies could change everything, or turn out to be too hard. [[@nuclear-fusion|Nuclear fusion]] copies the way the Sun shines, by squeezing atoms together. Experiments have released bursts of energy, but power plants are not expected before the 2040s, and maybe later.

Green hydrogen, made by splitting water with renewable electricity, could fuel steel plants, ships and lorries. Right now it is expensive. India launched a National Green Hydrogen Mission in 2023 to make it cheaper, aiming to produce about 5 million tonnes a year by 2030. Scientists are also working on tidal power, [[geothermal|geothermal]] heat from deep underground and space-based solar panels, though no one knows which will work at large scale.

By 2050, today's 10-year-olds will be in their mid-thirties. They may drive electric cars, cook on induction stoves and live in homes with panels on the roof. The air in cities like Delhi and Los Angeles could be much cleaner. The biggest change might be invisible: fewer greenhouse gases warming the planet. That is the real reason behind the whole shift, and why [[@climate-change|climate change]] and energy are two halves of the same story.

text: AI will almost certainly change many jobs. Whether it will leave fewer jobs overall is something experts strongly disagree about.

In 2025, the World Economic Forum surveyed more than a thousand large companies around the world. Their forecast was that by 2030, about 170 million new jobs would be created and about 92 million would disappear. That would leave more jobs than before. But forecasts like this are guesses, and many economists say the true numbers could be very different.
What most experts do agree on is this: AI is better at some tasks than others. Jobs are made of many tasks. A machine may take over some of them, and change what people spend their days doing.

st.prompt: When ATMs spread across the US from the 1970s, what happened to the number of human bank tellers?

options.t: It kept rising for years
It dropped to almost zero
It fell by half straight away

st.reveal: ATMs made each branch cheaper to run, so banks opened more branches. Tellers spent less time counting cash and more time helping customers. Teller numbers only began to fall decades later, as online banking grew.

James Bessen (2015), Learning by Doing, Yale University Press.
US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook.
n.certNote: Nobody knows how AI will change work. Some economists expect it to create more jobs than it removes, as past technologies did. Others think AI is different because it can do many kinds of thinking work at once.

History shows that new machines often destroy some jobs while creating others, and total work has usually grown. But the change can be very hard for the people whose jobs disappear, and AI may not follow the old pattern.
